title: Trade Deflection Index
text:
Trade Deflection Index (TDI)
      
    

    
      
    
  







  
    About the Trade Deflection Index

    
      When a major trading partner imposes tariffs, the exports of affected goods may be
      redirected towards other destinations. This reallocation of exports away from a
      tariff-imposing market toward third-country markets, within the same product lines,
      is known as trade deflection. The Trade Deflection Index (TDI) monitors the extent to
      which reduced exports to the tariff-imposing market are offset by increased exports of
      the same products to third markets. The figures presented here focus on exports
      originating in China, tracking their reallocation to markets other than the United
      States since the 2025 changes in U.S. trade policy.
    

    
    
    
    

    

    
      
        What does it measure?i
          Formal definition
          $$ TDI_{p,k,t} \;=\; \frac{\Delta \bar{X}^{\,i\to k}_{p,t}}{\Delta \bar{X}^{\,i\to j}_{p,t}} $$
          
            The numerator is the year-on-year change in exports to a third market,
            \( \Delta \bar{X}^{\,i\to k}_{p,t} = \bar{X}^{\,i\to k}_{p,t} - \bar{X}^{\,i\to k}_{p,t-12} \).
            The denominator is the year-on-year change in exports to the tariff-imposing market,
            \( \Delta \bar{X}^{\,i\to j}_{p,t} = \bar{X}^{\,i\to j}_{p,t-12} - \bar{X}^{\,i\to j}_{p,t} \),
            defined for products experiencing a decline (\( \Delta \bar{X}^{\,i\to j}_{p,t} > 0 \)).
            Written as prior minus current, the loss enters as a positive quantity, so the index is
            positive when losses are offset by gains in third markets.
          
          
            \(i\)origin country (China, fixed)
            \(j\)tariff-imposing country (United States, fixed)
            \(k\)third-country destination
            \(p\)product (HS 6-digit)
            \(t\)month
            \(\bar{X}\)three-month moving-average exports
          
        
        
          The index is the ratio of the change in exports of a tariff-affected country to
          third markets relative to the decrease in exports of the same products (at the
          HS 6-digit level) to the tariff-imposing market. It is defined for products that
          experienced losses in the tariff-imposing market to capture the idea of possible
          trade deflection. The numerator can be positive or negative, capturing either
          gains or losses in third markets. Changes are computed on a year-on-year basis
          using three-month moving averages to account for seasonality and smooth
          short-term volatility.
        
      
      
        How is it interpreted?i
          Reading the index
          
              
                Reading the magnitude
                The index value has an intuitive interpretation:
                
                  
                    
                    
                    
                    
                    
                    0
                    1
                    
                    
                    
                    No deflection
                    contraction across markets
                    Possible partial deflection
                    offsets part of the U.S. loss
                    Possible strong deflection
                    fully offsets or exceeds the loss
                  
                
              
              
              
                Aggregating across products, markets and time
                
                  Because every component shares the same denominator — total exports lost in the U.S. market —
                  the index sums cleanly across products, third markets and time:
                
                $$ TDI_{G,T} \;=\; \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{t\in T}\ \sum_{(p,k)\in G}\ \Delta \bar{X}^{\,i\to k}_{p,t}}
                                        {\displaystyle\sum_{t\in T}\ \sum_{p\in P}\ \Delta \bar{X}^{\,i\to j}_{p,t}} $$
                
                  where \(G\) is the grouping of interest — a sector, a country, a region, or all products and
                  destinations combined; \(P\) the full set of products that lost ground in the U.S. market;
                  and \(T\) the period. Taking \(T\) as a single month gives the index tracked over time, while
                  taking \(T\) as the whole period since February 2025 gives a cumulative figure. Because the
                  denominator runs over all loss-making products and is common to every grouping, each group's
                  value is its contribution to the total offset, and the contributions add up to the overall
                  index.
                
              
            
        
        
          The index captures, in dollar terms, the extent of offset in third markets for
          every US$1 of exports lost in the U.S. market. Values above zero indicate
          possible trade deflection, while negative values indicate a contraction across
          markets. It is a simple, non-causal metric, and other structural and non-tariff
          factors could drive observed patterns. Index components can be aggregated across
          products, sectors, third markets and time, where a common global denominator lets
          group-specific values be read as contributions to the total.
        
      
    
  





  
    Trade Deflection Figures

    
    
      
      
        
          
            Figure
            i
              How the selection works
              This figure breaks the deflection index down along two lines: geography (income → region → country) and industry (sector → product). You build a view by choosing values on either line.
              On each dropdown, leaving it on "select" ignores that level. Picking a single value filters the chart to it. Choosing "all" breaks the chart down into that level's parts (for example, all regions, or all sectors).
              Country and sector let you pick several at once to compare them side by side, up to ten. Picking "all sectors" shows the top ten in the current scope and offers the rest through download.
              One line can break down while the other filters — for instance, all regions within a single sector. The two lines cannot both break down at the same time, so the chart will ask you to narrow one.
              Choosing a single country sets its income and region for you; you can still change them.
